results.title: Nigeria and the United States have pledged stronger intelligence sharing and law enforcement cooperation against cybercrime, sextortion and
results.description:
Nigeria and the United States have pledged stronger intelligence sharing and law enforcement cooperation against cybercrime, sextortion and romance scams. During Nigeria’s Cybercrime Awareness Week in Abuja, US Deputy Assistant Secretary of State Michael Gonzales met officials from @officialEFCC, the National Security Adviser’s office, @ndlea_nigeria and @PoliceNG, urging closer coordination to tackle criminals operating across borders.

Gonzales said cooperation must move beyond arrests to dismantle criminal networks and trace their finances. FBI’s Abuja office and Nigerian authorities have secured 41 extraditions since 2022, including five in 2026. In August, Nigeria extradited two alleged cybercriminals in separate sextortion cases involving US minors.

results.title: Nigeria and the United States are intensifying their fight against cross-border cybercrime, romance scams and financially motivated sextorti
results.description:
Nigeria and the United States are intensifying their fight against cross-border cybercrime, romance scams and financially motivated sextortion.

The EFCC and FBI have facilitated 41 extraditions since 2022, including five completed in 2026, according to the US Mission.

But authorities say the next phase must go beyond arresting individual suspects.

The focus is now on dismantling the wider criminal networks, tracing their financial channels and targeting those who enable these operations.

For Nigerians, the challenge is clear: online fraud is increasingly international, and fighting it requires cooperation across borders.

The real measure of success should be fewer victims, disrupted criminal networks and successful prosecutions.

results.title: Why Nigerians Are Watching the U.S.
results.description:
Why Nigerians Are Watching the U.S. Midterms So Closely

As Americans voted in the 2026 midterm elections, the results are being followed with unusual intensity in Nigeria, where global conflict, fuel costs, and immigration policy have turned U.S. congressional races into a matter of direct national concern. The war involving Iran has pushed Brent crude above $100 a barrel, and President Trump has said elevated energy prices are unlikely to fall until after the November midterms. For Nigeria, where petrol prices remain tightly linked to international crude and refined product costs, that directly affects transport, food, and household living expenses, and analysts warn a sustained oil shock could undermine recent economic progress just as Nigeria enters its own 2027 election season. Because U.S. congressional control can influence the trajectory of the conflict and broader energy policy, many Nigerians see the midterms as a factor in whether fuel prices will eventually ease.
Immigration is the second major driver of interest. The United States is home to a large Nigerian diaspora, and recent immigration restrictions have made U.S. visa and green card policies a live issue for families, students, and professionals. The midterms could influence congressional scrutiny of immigration restrictions, visa policies, and arrangements requiring African countries to accept deportees all of which carry implications for Nigerian students, workers, and diaspora communities. The diaspora is also heavily invested in U.S. domestic issues such as immigration reform, healthcare, and inflation, meaning the results will directly alter their daily economic and legal landscape. Beyond these immediate concerns, the elections will shape congressional oversight of U.S. foreign assistance and security cooperation with Nigeria, a key counterterrorism partner and major aid recipient, while the next Congress will also have a role in the future implementation and potential reform of the African Growth and Opportunity Act, which provides duty free access to the U.S. market for Nigerian exports. With Nigeria ranking as the United States’ second largest trade partner in sub Saharan Africa, decisions made in Washington carry tangible consequences for Nigerian businesses and jobs. For many Nigerians, the midterms are no longer a distant American ritual but a referendum on the forces that shape the price of fuel at the pump, the fate of relatives abroad, and the economic ties that bind Africa’s most populous nation to Washington.

Evidence Cited for Declaring Nigeria a State Sponsor of Terrorism Over Video of Uniformed Youths Chanting Attacks on Infidels

A video of Nigerian military-uniformed youths has been presented as clear evidence for the United States and #Finland to declare Nigeria a state sponsor of terrorism. 

The footage shows a marching group in cadet uniforms reciting aggressive lyrics that call for AK47s to attack “infidels” in Enugu and Jos on a Sunday while “spraying fire” during what appear to be church activities. 

The group is described as wearing Nigerian pro-jihadist Cadet uniforms and referencing intentions to carry out Christian Genocide in Jos, Enugu, and targeting non-Muslims more broadly. This is a clear evidence of persistent threats amid reported violence against Christians.

The people of #Biafra question Rep. Riley Moore’s @RepRileyMoore support for ongoing US-Nigeria security cooperation in light of the video. Rep. R.Moore has repeatedly stated that the US-Nigeria security partnership remains ongoing, including activities of the kind shown in the footage. This raises the question of whether such cooperation is connected to the persistence of the Christian Genocide.

Rep. Moore has advocated for bilateral security frameworks while recommending the reintegration of Boko Haram, ISIS, and Fulani militants—who carry out attacks on Christian communities in Nigeria’s Middle Belt and Northeast—back into society. This has included meetings with Nigerian jihadist officials.

The video is not presented as a mistake or isolated incident. 

The man training the young militants was himself trained as a young militant with this jihadist ideology. 

The lyrics of the song they are chanting are not his own; the lyrics come from the Nigerian Ministry of Defense.

On this basis, the call is made US and Finland for Nigeria to be declared a state sponsor of terrorism.

We are calling @SecRubio, @alexstubb, @nayibbukele, @POTUS, @WalidPhares, and @RepNancyMace , @RepBarryMoore in connection with the demand.
